science.title: HFPnet: a hybrid feature perception network for high-quality low-light light field enhancement
science.description: Existing algorithms for low-light light field enhancement (L3FE) generally suffer from detail loss, severe noise interference and poor cross-view consistency, which greatly degrade the reconstruction quality of L3FE. To solve these problems, the hybrid feature perception network (HFPnet) is proposed for high-quality L3FE. Firstly, a hybrid decoupling module (HDM) is designed to extract spatial features, angular features and omnidirectional EPI geometric features of light field (LF) images. Based on HDM, three dedicated optimization modules are constructed, including a reflection estimation module (REM), a gradient prior module (GPM) and an illumination estimation module (IEM). These modules collaboratively compensate for missing texture details, suppress image noise and restore distorted illumination information to achieve high-fidelity L3FE and stable cross-view consistency. Extensive experimental results verify that the proposed HFPnet outperforms current state-of-the-art (SOTA) algorithms.

science.title: New math tools reveal brain activity more accurately by correcting noisy calcium signals
science.description: When a firework bursts in the sky, what often follows is a cloud of smoke in the shape of the firework—a visual echo that lingers long after the spectacular explosion itself is over. A similar phenomenon happens in the brain when a neuron fires: The explosion of activity causes a change in calcium levels, resulting in fluorescence that neuroscientists use as a proxy for brain activity. Unfortunately, however, much like that cloud of smoke, the calcium indicator only approximates the original's shape, size and origin.

science.title: FBBDL: flow-aware benign-behavior deviation learning for leakage-controlled unseen-family DoS detection
science.description: Detecting previously unseen denial-of-service (DoS) attack families remains challenging because conventional random or stratified splits may allow family-specific information to influence model development, while imbalanced attack distributions can bias detection toward dominant families. This study proposes Flow-Aware Benign-Behavior Deviation Learning (FBBDL), a leakage-controlled framework for unseen-family DoS detection using aggregated network-flow statistics. FBBDL excludes every bin containing a target-family flow from all development stages and integrates duplicate-group-disjoint cross-fitted benign-deviation estimation, tempered family-frequency weighting, nested pseudo-unseen-family validation, and development-only false-positive-rate (FPR) control. Experiments on 692,692 eligible flows from the Wednesday CIC-IDS2017 capture evaluated four independently withheld DoS families over 20 matched seeds. FBBDL achieved a macro recall of 95.64%, a macro geometric mean (G-mean) of 0.975, and a worst-family G-mean of 0.958, with a mean benign FPR of 0.62%. Compared with class-weighted XGBoost (CW-XGB), the strongest evaluated baseline, FBBDL improved macro and worst-family G-mean by 0.016 and 0.033, respectively; the paired differences remained significant after Holm correction ((p < 0.001)). Ablation experiments identified multi-flow temporal aggregation as the dominant contributor, with additional gains from benign-reference deviation, family-frequency weighting, and nested family withholding. Sensitivity analyses further indicated stable performance across the evaluated aggregation and balancing settings. The frozen detector required 0.81 ms per aggregated bin, corresponding to approximately 1,235 bins per second. An independent Wednesday-to-Friday transfer evaluation revealed important limitations: although DDoS score ranking remained strong (normalized pAUROC@1% = 0.997), the frozen threshold produced a benign FPR of 30.23%, exceeding the 1% operating target, while PortScan recall was only 0.14%. These findings support the effectiveness of FBBDL under the evaluated within-capture family-withheld setting, while demonstrating that reliable cross-capture operation cannot be inferred from score-ranking performance alone.
